1:
A householder of Sāvatthī went forth after his wife died. Before that he built his own room, fire-room and storeroom,
filled with ghee and rice; even as a monk he had his servants cook whatever he liked.
2:
He owned so much that he had separate robes for day and night. Seeing his robes and rugs laid out to dry,
visiting monks asked whose they were. “All mine,” he said.
3: “The Blessed One allows only three robes,” they said, and took him, unwilling, to the Buddha.
4:
The Buddha asked, “Why keep so much? Do I not praise wanting little and contentment?”
Angry, the monk threw off his outer robe and stood among them in a single robe.
5:
The Buddha said, “Even as a demon long ago, you sought shame and fear of wrong for twelve years.”
His shame returned; he put his robe back on and bowed. The monks asked him to tell that story.
6:
Long ago, when Brahmadatta reigned in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born to the chief queen as Prince Mahisāsa.
When he could walk, his brother Prince Canda was born.
7:
The queen died and the king took a new chief queen, who bore Prince Sūriya. Delighted, the king said,
“I grant you a boon for your son.” She kept it to use later.
8:
When the princes were grown, she asked, “Give my son the kingdom.” The king refused: “My two sons
shine like blazing fires; how can I give it to your son?” But she kept on asking.
9:
Fearing she might harm them, the king called his two sons: “Go and live in the forest;
after my death, come back and rule.” Weeping, the princes bowed to him and left.
10:
Prince Sūriya, playing in the courtyard, saw them go and said, “I’ll go with my brothers,”
and the three entered the Himalayan forest.
11:
The Bodhisatta left the path, sat under a tree and said,
“Sūriya, go to that lake, bathe and drink, and bring us water in lotus leaves.”
12:
A water-demon held that lake by a grant from Vessavaṇa, the great deva-king of the north:
he might seize anyone who entered the water, except those who knew the divine virtues — but no one who stayed out.
13:
Sūriya waded in without a thought. The demon seized him: “Do you know the divine virtues?”
“The sun and the moon,” he said. “You do not know,” said the demon, and dragged him to his home under the water.
14:
When Sūriya did not return, the Bodhisatta sent Canda. Seized too, Canda answered, “The four directions,”
and was dragged away with the words, “You do not know.”
15:
Going himself, the Bodhisatta saw footprints going into the water but none coming out.
Knowing a demon held the lake, he armed himself with sword and bow and stood without entering.
16:
Since he would not enter, the demon came disguised as a forest worker and coaxed him:
“You must be weary. Go in, bathe and drink, eat lotus roots, wear flowers, and rest at ease.”
17:
The Bodhisatta saw through him. Asked whether he knew the divine virtues, he said,
“I can tell you them — but not while my body is soiled.”
18:
The demon bathed him, fed him, anointed and garlanded him,
and seated him on a high couch in a flower-decked pavilion.
19:
With the demon at his feet he said, “Listen well,” and spoke this verse:
“Those endowed with shame and fear of wrong, possessed of bright qualities,
the calm, true people in the world — these are called ‘divine in virtue’.”
20:
Shame of wrongdoing (hiri) arises from looking at oneself; fear of wrongdoing (ottappa) arises from fear
of the blame of the wise and of a bad rebirth. These two are the root of all good qualities.
21: Pleased, the demon said, “I will return one brother. Which shall I bring?” “The youngest,” said the Bodhisatta.
22:
“You only know the divine virtues; you do not live by them,” said the demon.
“You pass over the elder for the younger and fail to honour your elder.”
23:
“We came to this forest because of him,” he answered. “His mother asked our father for the kingdom,
and our father sent us here to keep us safe. Yet this boy followed us.”
24:
“If I went home and said, ‘A demon ate him in the forest,’ no one would believe me.
Fearing that blame, I asked for him first.”
25:
“Well done! You both know the divine virtues and live by them.”
Delighted, the demon brought back both brothers.
26:
The Bodhisatta admonished him: “Through past evil you were born a flesh-eating demon.
From now on give up evil and do good.” In time the demon was tamed.
27:
Seeing in the stars that his father had died, the Bodhisatta returned to Bārāṇasī with the demon and became king.
He made Canda viceroy and Sūriya commander of the army.
28:
He built a shrine for the demon in a lovely place, where it received the finest garlands, flowers and food.
He ruled righteously and passed on according to his deeds.
29:
The Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths, and the monk attained stream-entry. “The demon was this monk;
Sūriya was Ānanda, Canda was Sāriputta, and the eldest, Prince Mahisāsa, was I myself.”
